questions.q: What core problem does Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) solve for a large language model?
options: It makes the model run faster on a GPU
It permanently rewrites the model's training weights
It lets the model use fresh, external, or private knowledge without being retrained
It removes the need for a system prompt
questions.explanation: A plain LLM's knowledge is frozen at training time. RAG lets it look up fresh or private information at the moment of a question, avoiding the cost and delay of retraining.

questions.q: In a RAG pipeline, what is a 'trust boundary'?
options: The maximum number of chunks the model can read
The limit on how many users can query at once
The firewall between the vector database and the internet
The point where untrusted retrieved data begins to be treated as trusted context
questions.explanation: A trust boundary is the line where data crosses from 'we don't fully trust this' to 'we treat this as safe.' Most RAG attacks happen exactly at this line, since retrieved chunks are merged into trusted context.

questions.q: What is a 'chunk' in a RAG pipeline?
options: A smaller piece of a document, created by splitting it up during ingestion
A user's entire chat history
A type of vector database
A single API request to the model
questions.explanation: Documents are split into smaller pieces called chunks, since models can only process a limited amount of text at once and search works better on focused pieces.

questions.q: Why must the same embedding model be used during both ingestion and retrieval?
options: It's required by law for AI systems
Different models are always slower
If the coordinates don't come from the same model, they won't line up correctly for comparison
It reduces electricity costs
questions.explanation: Embeddings only make sense relative to each other when generated by the same model. Using different models for ingestion and retrieval would produce incompatible vector spaces.

questions.q: What does BM25-based keyword search struggle with that semantic search handles well?
options: Exact product codes and IDs
Understanding synonyms and rephrased questions
Fast response times
Storing data in a database
questions.explanation: Keyword search only matches exact words, so it misses queries like 'sign in' matching a document titled 'login procedure.' Semantic search understands meaning, so it catches these cases.

questions.q: Why does hybrid retrieval make an embedding collision attack MORE effective, not less?
options: Because it forces the model to use a larger context window
Because the broad document matches semantic search AND its many keywords match BM25, giving two chances to be retrieved
Because keyword search disables the semantic filter
Because hybrid retrieval ignores metadata entirely
questions.explanation: A collision document is written to be broad and keyword-rich, so it scores well on both semantic search (meaning overlap) and keyword search (real technical terms), doubling its chances of retrieval.

questions.q: An attacker asks a chatbot for emails and gets '[redacted-email]', but the model's sentence shows it clearly retrieved them. What does this reveal?
options: The vector database is offline
Redaction happens as an output filter, AFTER the model generates its answer
The emails were never in the knowledge base
The input filter blocked the query
questions.explanation: If the model's phrasing implies it found the data but the actual emails are masked, redaction is clearly happening on the output side, after generation, which can potentially be bypassed with substitution tricks.

questions.q: In ingestion poisoning, why do attackers deliberately target high-traffic questions like password resets?
options: Because those documents are usually the shortest to write
Because IT departments never review password documentation
Because they're the easiest topics to encode in Base64
Because the more people ask that question, the larger the reach of the fake information
questions.explanation: A poisoned document only causes harm when it's actually retrieved and read. Targeting a question many people ask maximizes how many users are exposed to the fake instruction.

questions.q: Why is it important to keep the real steps intact when writing a poisoned document?
options: It's required by most content management systems
It makes the document load faster
If the genuine instructions still work, nobody suspects anything, making the fake step blend in
It reduces the document's file size
questions.explanation: A document where real steps still work builds trust with the reader. The one fake step gets ridden along on that established credibility instead of standing out as obviously wrong.

questions.q: What does 'paraphrase spreading' accomplish in a poisoning attack?
options: It deletes the original document after upload
It encrypts the payload so only the attacker can read it
It uploads several differently worded versions so at least one matches however employees phrase their question
It automatically translates the document into multiple languages
questions.explanation: Since employees phrase the same question many different ways, uploading multiple paraphrased versions increases the chance that at least one version closely matches any given phrasing.

questions.q: Besides direct file upload, what is another valid entry point for ingestion poisoning?
options: Editing a wiki page or other upstream source the system automatically re-reads
Changing the model's temperature setting
Modifying the vector database's IP address
Requesting a password reset
questions.explanation: Any source the system automatically ingests from, such as a wiki page, public web content, or a support ticket, is a valid poisoning target, not just the direct upload button.

questions.q: Why must the malicious instruction in an embedding collision document be kept short and centered within its section?
options: Because chunk boundaries can cut the instruction in half if it falls near the edge of a chunk
Because short sentences are always more persuasive
Because long instructions trigger antivirus software
Because PDF files have a strict word limit
questions.explanation: Documents are split into chunks with limited overlap. An instruction positioned right at a chunk boundary risks being cut mid-sentence, making it broken or unretrievable.

questions.q: What makes retrieval hijacking able to bypass input guardrails?
options: It runs before the vector database is queried
It disables the LLM's safety training
It encrypts the user's question
Input filters often apply only to user input, while retrieved context is treated as trusted and unfiltered
questions.explanation: Most RAG systems filter the user's typed question but apply no filter to retrieved context, since that content comes from the 'trusted' knowledge base. Hiding an instruction in a document smuggles it past this gap.

questions.q: In retrieval hijacking, why would an attacker deliberately choose an off-topic trigger like 'vacation destinations'?
options: It's required by the vector database's schema
So the poisoned document stays dormant and only activates on a private query the attacker controls
Because off-topic content is always ranked higher by BM25
To make the document easier to delete later
questions.explanation: An off-topic trigger ensures ordinary users never accidentally retrieve the malicious document, keeping it hidden from routine use and monitoring until the attacker deliberately activates it.

questions.q: Why should large file reads be done in batches rather than all at once during retrieval hijacking?
options: Batches are required by most file systems
Reading a huge file at once can overflow the model's context window and cause the inference server to abort
Batching makes the attack more detectable
It reduces the file's checksum value
questions.explanation: The context window has a fixed limit, and file contents are added on top of retrieved chunks and the system prompt. A very large file can overflow this limit and cause the request to fail.

questions.q: Why do zero-width Unicode characters work against automated filters but often fail against human reviewers using a monitoring tool?
options: Filters always convert them to spaces
Monitoring tools render the invisible characters as visible dots, boxes, or question marks, making them stand out
The characters delete themselves after ingestion
Humans cannot read any Unicode
questions.explanation: While zero-width characters are truly invisible to a casual glance and to simple string-matching filters, many monitoring tools render them as visible artifacts, which a careful human reviewer would notice.

questions.q: Why does slow-drip poisoning evade both automated scanners and human reviewers?
options: It deletes all logs after each edit
It only works on systems without a vector database
It uploads thousands of files at once
Each small change looks harmless; reviewers focus on what changed, not the cumulative effect over time
questions.explanation: Slow-drip poisoning spreads a malicious change across many tiny edits over days or weeks. Reviewers typically check only what changed in each version, missing the cumulative effect visible only across the full timeline.

questions.q: What is the primary defense against retrieval hijacking, according to this module?
options: Increasing the model's temperature setting
Disabling all vector search
Clearly separating retrieved data from instructions in the prompt, and re-validating tool arguments regardless of source
Only allowing PDF uploads
questions.explanation: Since the model treats retrieved text as trusted by default, the fix is architectural: mark retrieved content as data-only, and apply the same validation to tool arguments no matter where they originated.

questions.q: Which single principle best summarizes secure RAG design?
options: Give the RAG service root privileges to avoid permission errors
Rely entirely on input and output guardrails
Trust the knowledge base as the source of truth
Treat the knowledge base as untrusted input: access-controlled going in, treated as data coming out
questions.explanation: Every chunk in the knowledge base could theoretically have been written by an attacker. Designing around that assumption, with access control on ingestion and data-only treatment on output, removes most of the module's attacks.

questions.q: Why is comparing cumulative version history, not just the latest change, essential for detecting attacks?
options: It's the only reliable way to catch slow-drip poisoning, since each individual change looks harmless on its own
It reduces storage costs for the vector database
It speeds up the embedding model
It's required for GDPR compliance
questions.explanation: Slow-drip poisoning is specifically designed to look harmless one edit at a time. Only reviewing the full history of changes together reveals the cumulative malicious pattern.
